title: What We're Into: Documentary debunks famous Bigfoot film
excerpt: The most famous piece of evidence touted as proving the existence of Bigfoot, about a minute of 16 mm color film allegedly exposed on Oct. 20, 1967, and subject since […]
content:
The most famous piece of evidence touted as proving the existence of Bigfoot, about a minute of 16 mm color film allegedly exposed on Oct. 20, 1967, and subject since to a level of scrutiny surpassed only by the Zapruder film of President Kennedy’s assassination, is tottering like a bridge built of spaghetti.

Al dente spaghetti.

I am discouraged.

Dismayed.

It’s as though we had discovered the Mona Lisa was actually a paint-by-numbers rendered by a Tuscan shepherd.

Or that Paul McCartney — the original version — really did die in 1966, as the conspiracy theorists insist, and was replaced by someone who not only was a doppelganger but who also wrote “Hey Jude” and “Blackbird,” thus surpassing the man he replaced.

The Patterson-Gimlin film was taken along Bluff Creek in Northern California. Its two namesakes are Roger Patterson, who was holding the camera, and Bob Gimlin, his partner in the Bigfoot search. Both were from Yakima, Washington.

In the nearly six decades since, the film has remained the chief exhibit for Bigfoot proponents, retaining its position no matter how many blurry photographs or plaster casts of large footprints or other videos are proffered.

I’ve been fascinated since I was a boy by the possibility that a hulking primate, unknown to science, roams the great woods of the Northwest.

As the years and decades have passed without unimpeachable proof — a body, obviously, or at least DNA that satisfies the scientists — the optimism I had as a child has changed to a gradually solidifying agnosticism.

In the pantheon of cryptids — unproven animals — Bigfoot is at least plausible, biologically speaking.

Even as I’ve grown more skeptical, the Patterson-Gimlin film continues to nag, the mental equivalent of a popcorn husk that wedges between molars and resists all attempts at extraction.

Some people branded the film as a hoax from the start.

In 2004 author Greg Long published “The Making of Bigfoot,” the most thorough and well-researched attempt to discredit the film.

But Long’s book, though persuasive, relied heavily on interviews, including with the man who claimed he wore the costume and walked past the Kodak camera Patterson was holding in 1967.

The new attack on the film’s authenticity is something else altogether. Something that doesn’t depend on the inevitably faulty memories of people, or their inclination to exaggerate or lie or simply be mistaken (problems which also plague the thousands of stories from people who believe they saw a Bigfoot).

Marq Evans’ documentary, “Capturing Bigfoot,” was released on Oct. 20 — which is no coincidence, that being the 59th anniversary of the film. The 103-minute documentary is available on Amazon Prime Video.

The documentary’s centerpiece, and the likely death knell for the Patterson-Gimlin film, is an even shorter clip of 16 mm film, about 40 seconds. This clip, about half of which is in the documentary, shows a figure similar, but not identical, to the subject in the Patterson-Gimlin film, walking closer to the camera while a man sits on a horse — a man several people who knew him said was Gimlin (who is still alive; Patterson died of cancer in 1972).

“Capturing Bigfoot” also includes an interview with Patterson’s widow, Patricia, and their son, Clint, who admit the 1967 film was a hoax involving a man wearing a suit.

The documentary doesn’t answer every question, to be sure.

The 40-second film, which Evans acquired from a woman whose father was involved with Patterson, carries a stamp that it was manufactured in 1966, the year before the Patterson-Gimlin film. There is no way to prove, though, when the 40-second clip was made.

The logical assumption, given the similarities in the hirsute figures in the two films and the apparent involvement of both Patterson and Gimlin, is that the shorter clip was part of a rehearsal for the famous 1967 film.

Even some renowned Bigfoot researchers reached that conclusion after watching “Capturing Bigfoot.”

Cliff Barackman and James “Bobo” Fay, two of the four stars of the Animal Planet show, “Finding Bigfoot,” both said on a recent episode of their podcast, “Bigfoot and Beyond,” that although they had considered the Patterson-Gimlin film authentic, they now consider it a probable hoax.

As I do.

Barackman and Fay point out that disproving the Patterson-Gimlin film, though a milestone in Bigfoot research, does not mean there is no such animal.

This is true.

But the reason the Patterson-Gimlin film retained its cachet through the decades was that not even the skeptics — and they are legion, especially among scientists — could make an overwhelming case for why it was a hoax. In particular they struggled to explain how Patterson and Gimlin, who had no experience in making costumes or filmmaking, managed, in 1967, to pull off what even many skeptics conceded was quite a sophisticated prank, one that lacked irrefutable proof that it was faked.

“Capturing Bigfoot,” with that film clip, is the proverbial smoking gun.

And although Evans doesn’t explain Patterson’s technique, that seems to me largely irrelevant.

The documentary convinces me that Patterson did hoax the 1967 film, even if I don’t know, and almost certainly never will know, how he did so.

Jayson Jacoby, editor, Baker City Herald.
